entries.lesson_core_move: Apply the continuous-time Fourier transform linearity property to compute the spectrum of a weighted sum of signals by carrying the same weights onto their transform-domain terms.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Scaled Signal

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)$ has CTFT $X(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $-5x(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: By CTFT linearity, the coefficient stays attached to the spectrum term, so scaling $x(t)$ by $-5$ gives $-5X(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $u(t)$ has CTFT $U(j\omega)$, find the CTFT of $4u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Linearity carries the scalar through unchanged, so multiplying $u(t)$ by $4$ multiplies its CTFT by $4$ as well.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Sum of Two Signals

prompt_blocks.text: Given that $p(t) \leftrightarrow P(j\omega)$ and $q(t) \leftrightarrow Q(j\omega)$, what is the CTFT of $p(t)+q(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use linearity term by term. Since $p(t) \leftrightarrow P(j\omega)$ and $q(t) \leftrightarrow Q(j\omega)$, the sum transforms to $P(j\omega)+Q(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given that $m(t) \leftrightarrow M(j\omega)$ and $n(t) \leftrightarrow N(j\omega)$, what is the CTFT of $m(t)+n(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Linearity keeps each known transform pair intact. The CTFT of $m(t)+n(t)$ is therefore the sum of the two spectra, $M(j\omega)+N(j\omega)$.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Weighted Sum of Two Signals

prompt_blocks.text: Given $p(t) \leftrightarrow P(j\omega)$ and $q(t) \leftrightarrow Q(j\omega)$, what is the CTFT of $4p(t)-5q(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use linearity term by term. Keep the $4$ with $p(t)$ and keep the $-5$ with $q(t)$, then transform each piece separately.
So the CTFT is $4P(j\omega)-5Q(j\omega)$. The coefficients stay attached to their own spectrum terms; they do not swap, combine, or become frequency scaling factors.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $u(t) \leftrightarrow U(j\omega)$ and $v(t) \leftrightarrow V(j\omega)$, what is the CTFT of $-3v(t)+2u(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply linearity to each weighted term separately. The $2$ stays with $u(t)$ and the $-3$ stays with $v(t)$, even though the terms are written in reverse order.
So the CTFT is $2U(j\omega)-3V(j\omega)$. The order of the terms does not matter, but each coefficient must stay attached to its own spectrum term.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Multi-Term Weighted Sum

prompt_blocks.text: Given $p(t) \leftrightarrow P(j\omega)$, $q(t) \leftrightarrow Q(j\omega)$, and $r(t) \leftrightarrow R(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $3p(t)+q(t)-2r(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use linearity term by term: keep each coefficient attached to its matching transform term. The result is $3P(j\omega)+Q(j\omega)-2R(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $m(t) \leftrightarrow M(j\omega)$, $n(t) \leftrightarrow N(j\omega)$, and $s(t) \leftrightarrow S(j\omega)$, compute the CTFT of $-2m(t)+5n(t)+3s(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply linearity to each term separately and carry the coefficients across unchanged. That gives $-2M(j\omega)+5N(j\omega)+3S(j\omega)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a time shift x(t - t0) into the Fourier-domain factor e^(-j omega t0) X(j omega) so known transform pairs can be reused in transform-property calculations.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Delayed Signal from a Known Pair

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t-3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay of $3$ multiplies the known spectrum by $e^{-j3\omega}$. Keep the original spectrum $X(j\omega)$ unchanged and attach the delay factor to it.

prompt_blocks.text: If $g(t) \leftrightarrow G(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $g(t-5)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay of $5$ multiplies the known spectrum by $e^{-j5\omega}$. The time shift does not change the base spectrum itself.

sections.section_title: Transforming an Advanced Signal from a Known Pair

prompt_blocks.text: If $e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{-2(t-4)}u(t-4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is the known causal exponential delayed by $4$, so the time-shift rule multiplies the base spectrum by $e^{-j4\omega}$. The denominator stays $2+j\omega$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $e^{-3t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{3+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{-3(t-1)}u(t-1)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same move: recognize a delay of $1$, keep the original transform pair, and attach the factor $e^{-j\omega}$. Only the shift amount changes.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Sign in the Time-Shift Factor

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what factor multiplies $X(j\omega)$ for $x(t+6)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plus sign means an advance, so rewrite $x(t+6)$ as $x(t-(-6))$ and read the shift amount as $t_0=-6$.
Substituting gives $e^{-j\omega(-6)}=e^{+j6\omega}$. The factor is positive because the signal advances.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what factor multiplies $X(j\omega)$ for $x(t-3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The minus sign means a delay, so here $t_0=3$.
Substituting $t_0=3$ gives $e^{-j3\omega}$. A delay uses the negative exponent.

sections.section_title: Applying Time Shifting to a Shifted Sum of Known Pairs

prompt_blocks.text: If $g(t)=4x(t-3)+5x(t+1)$ and $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is $G(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the sum term by term. A delay of $3$ contributes $e^{-j3\omega}$, and an advance of $1$ contributes $e^{+j\omega}$. Keep the coefficients attached to their own terms, then combine the transformed pieces.

prompt_blocks.text: If $h(t)=2x(t-4)-x(t+1)+3x(t-2)$ and $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is $H(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Treat each term separately. The delay of $4$ gives $e^{-j4\omega}$, the advance of $1$ gives $e^{+j\omega}$, and the delay of $2$ gives $e^{-j2\omega}$. The negative coefficient stays with the middle term, and all three transformed pieces share $X(j\omega)$.

entries.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
entries.lesson_core_move: Determine how a time shift leaves the Fourier-transform magnitude unchanged while adding the linear phase term -omega t0 to the spectrum.

sections.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
sections.section_title: Magnitude Spectrum of a Time-Shifted Signal

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $y(t)=x(t-5)$, what is $|Y(j\omega)|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time delay multiplies the Fourier transform by a complex exponential.
That factor has unit magnitude, so taking the magnitude removes it and leaves the spectrum unchanged.
So the magnitude spectrum is $|X(j\omega)|$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $|X(j\omega)|=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\omega^2}}$ and $y(t)=x(t+3)$, what is $|Y(j\omega)|$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An advance is still a time shift, so rewrite it as $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$ with $t_0=-3$.
The factor $e^{j3\omega}$ has unit magnitude, so the magnitude spectrum does not change.
So the correct magnitude is the same as the original one.

sections.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
sections.section_title: Phase Change from a Time Delay

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle X(j\omega)=-\omega/4$ and $y(t)=x(t-5)$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A delay of $5$ adds $-5\omega$ to the original phase, so $\angle Y(j\omega)=\angle X(j\omega)-5\omega=-\omega/4-5\omega=-21\omega/4$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $\angle X(j\omega)=3\omega/2$ and $y(t)=x(t+2)$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: An advance by $2$ means $t_0=-2$, so the shift term is $-\omega t_0=+2\omega$. Then $\angle Y(j\omega)=3\omega/2+2\omega=7\omega/2$.

sections.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
sections.section_title: Phase Change from a Time Advance

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $\angle X(j\omega)=\omega/3$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$ for $y(t)=x(t+2)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time advance by $2$ multiplies the spectrum by $e^{j2\omega}$, so the phase gains $+2\omega$ while the magnitude stays unchanged.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$ and $\angle X(j\omega)=-\omega/4$, what is $\angle Y(j\omega)$ for $y(t)=x(t+4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A time advance by $4$ multiplies the spectrum by $e^{j4\omega}$, so the phase gains $+4\omega$ while the magnitude stays unchanged.

sections.lesson_title: Magnitude and Phase Effects of Time Shifting
sections.section_title: Identifying a Time Shift from Linear Phase

prompt_blocks.text: If $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)e^{-j6\omega}$, what time shift does $y(t)$ represent relative to $x(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: The magnitude changes, so the shift cannot be read.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Match the factor to the standard shift form $e^{-j\omega t_0}$. Here $e^{-j6\omega}=e^{-j\omega t_0}$, so $t_0=6$.
A positive $t_0$ means a delay, so $y(t)=x(t-6)$. The factor has unit magnitude, so $|Y(j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)|$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)e^{j3\omega}e^{j\pi/4}$, what time shift does $y(t)$ represent relative to $x(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: The magnitude changes, so the shift cannot be read.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Ignore the constant phase offset $e^{j\pi/4}$; it does not affect the time shift. Match $e^{j3\omega}$ to $e^{-j\omega t_0}$, so $t_0=-3$.
A negative $t_0$ means an advance, so $y(t)=x(t+3)$. The magnitude is unchanged.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a known Fourier transform pair for x(t) into the transform of x(at) by applying reciprocal frequency scaling and the 1/|a| magnitude factor.

sections.section_title: Transforming x(2t) from a Known Fourier Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the time-scaling rule $x(at) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{|a|}X\left(j\frac{\omega}{a}\right)$ with $a=3$. The frequency variable becomes $\omega/3$, and the spectrum picks up the factor $1/3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $g(t) \leftrightarrow G(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $g(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same rule with $a=4$: $g(at) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{|a|}G\left(j\frac{\omega}{a}\right)$. So $g(4t)$ has transform $\frac14 G\left(j\frac{\omega}{4}\right)$.

sections.section_title: Transforming x(t/2) from a Known Fourier Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Treat $x(t/3)$ as $x(at)$ with $a=\frac{1}{3}$. The time-scaling rule gives a factor of $\frac{1}{|1/3|}=3$ and compresses the frequency argument to $3\omega$, so the transform is $3X(j3\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t/4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Treat $x(t/4)$ as $x(at)$ with $a=\frac{1}{4}$. The time-scaling rule gives a factor of $\frac{1}{|1/4|}=4$ and compresses the frequency argument to $4\omega$, so the transform is $4X(j4\omega)$.

sections.section_title: Applying the 1/|a| Magnitude Factor

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $5x(2t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the outside scalar $5$ multiplying the time-scaled signal $x(2t)$. First apply the time-scaling rule with $a=2$, then carry the scalar through unchanged.
So the transform is $\frac{5}{2}X\left(j\frac{\omega}{2}\right)$. The outside scalar multiplies the $1/|a|$ factor, and the reciprocal frequency substitution stays the same.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, find the Fourier transform of $3x(5t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the scale factor $a=5$ inside $x(5t)$. Apply time scaling first, then multiply the result by the outside scalar $3$.

So the transform is $\frac{3}{5}X\left(j\frac{\omega}{5}\right)$. The coefficient stays attached to the amplitude, while the time-scale factor contributes the reciprocal frequency change and the $1/|a|$ magnitude factor.

sections.section_title: Using Time Scaling with a General Scale Factor

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the time-scaling rule with $a=3$: $x(at) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{|a|}X\left(j\frac{\omega}{a}\right)$.
The correct choice keeps both parts of the rule: reciprocal frequency scaling and the $1/|a|$ factor. The other choices either scale the frequency in the wrong direction or drop the magnitude factor.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(-2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Here $a=-2$, so the rule gives $1/|a|=1/2$ and $\omega/a=-\omega/2$.
The negative coefficient option incorrectly uses $1/a$ instead of $1/|a|$. The other choices either miss the sign reversal, reverse frequency in the wrong direction, or drop the magnitude factor.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a known Fourier transform pair x(t) <-> X(j omega) into the time-reversed pair x(-t) <-> X(-j omega).

sections.section_title: Reversing a Known Transform Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Given the known pair $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{3+j\omega}$, which pair is $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time reversal flips both the time variable and the frequency variable. If $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, then $x(-t) \leftrightarrow X(-j\omega)$.
That matches choice A. The other choices either leave the spectrum unchanged or fail to reverse the signal correctly.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the known pair $x(t)=2e^{-t}u(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)=\frac{2}{1+j\omega}$, which pair is $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Time reversal keeps the coefficient and flips the sign in the exponent and in the frequency variable. So $x(-t)$ is the anti-causal version of the signal, and the spectrum becomes $X(-j\omega)$.
That is choice A. The other options either leave the spectrum unchanged or fail to reverse the time-domain signal correctly.

sections.section_title: Replacing Frequency Signs in a Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: If $X(j\omega)=(1+j)\frac{1-j\omega}{3+j\omega}$, what is the spectrum of $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Replace $\omega$ by $-\omega$ everywhere in the spectrum. The outside factor $(1+j)$ stays unchanged, and each $j\omega$ changes sign.
So the spectrum of $x(-t)$ is $(1+j)\frac{1+j\omega}{3-j\omega}$. The coefficients stay attached; only the frequency signs flip.

prompt_blocks.text: If $X(j\omega)=\frac{4+2j\omega}{1-5j\omega}$, what is the spectrum of $x(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Negate $\omega$ everywhere in the explicit spectrum. That flips the sign on every $j\omega$ term, but it does not change the constants.
So the time-reversed spectrum is $\frac{4-2j\omega}{1+5j\omega}$. The correct move is sign replacement, not leaving the spectrum unchanged or flipping only one part.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Reflected Signals Before Applying Time Reversal

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ has transform $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{3+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{3t}u(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Recognize $e^{3t}u(-t)$ as the reflected signal $x(-t)$ for the base pair $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$. Time reversal changes $X(j\omega)$ to $X(-j\omega)$ and nothing else.
So the reflected signal has transform $X(-j\omega)=\frac{1}{3-j\omega}$. The key step is spotting the reflected form first, then applying the sign flip.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)=2e^{-4t}u(t)$ has transform $X(j\omega)=\frac{2}{4+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $2e^{4t}u(-t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: $2e^{4t}u(-t)$ is just $x(-t)$ for the known pair $x(t)=2e^{-4t}u(t)$. Once that reflection is recognized, the frequency variable changes sign and the amplitude stays the same.

Therefore $x(-t)=2e^{4t}u(-t)$ has transform $X(-j\omega)=\frac{2}{4-j\omega}$. The wrong choices either leave the spectrum unchanged, lose the factor of 2, or confuse reflection with scaling or shifting.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert multiplication by a complex exponential in time into the corresponding shift of X(j omega) along the continuous-frequency axis.

sections.section_title: Shifting X(j omega) to X(j(omega - omega0))

prompt_blocks.text: Given $g(t) \leftrightarrow G(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $g(t)e^{j2\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A positive exponential in time shifts the spectrum to the right. Replace $\omega$ with $\omega-2\omega_0$, so the result is $G(j(\omega-2\omega_0))$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t)e^{j\omega_1 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiplying by $e^{j\omega_1 t}$ shifts the spectrum to the right by $\omega_1$. The Fourier transform is the original spectrum evaluated at $\omega-\omega_1$, so the answer is $X(j(\omega-\omega_1))$.

sections.section_title: Shifting X(j omega) to X(j(omega + omega0))

prompt_blocks.text: Given $g(t) \leftrightarrow G(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $g(t)e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiplying by $e^{-j2\omega_0 t}$ shifts the spectrum left by $2\omega_0$, so you replace $\omega$ with $\omega+2\omega_0$ inside $G(j\omega)$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t) \leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, what is the Fourier transform of $x(t)e^{-j3\omega_0 t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative exponential means a leftward frequency shift, so the Fourier transform is the original spectrum evaluated at $\omega+3\omega_0$.

sections.section_title: Applying a Numeric Frequency Shift to a Known Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Given $e^{-2t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{-2t}u(t)e^{j5t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Multiply by $e^{j5t}$, so shift the known spectrum to the right by $5$ and replace $\omega$ with $\omega-5$. The transform is $\frac{1}{2+j(\omega-5)}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $e^{-3t}u(t) \leftrightarrow \frac{1}{3+j\omega}$, what is the Fourier transform of $e^{-3t}u(t)e^{j2t}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $e^{j2t}$ shifts the spectrum to the right by $2$, so the known pair becomes $\frac{1}{3+j(\omega-2)}$.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Correct Shift Direction from the Modulating Exponential

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t) \leftrightarrow Y(j\omega)$, what is $\mathcal{F}\{y(t)e^{-j\omega_1 t}\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The negative modulating exponential shifts the spectrum left, so the frequency argument gains $\omega_1$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t) \leftrightarrow Y(j\omega)$, what is $\mathcal{F}\{y(t)e^{j\omega_1 t}\}$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The positive modulating exponential shifts the spectrum right, so subtract $\omega_1$ inside the frequency argument.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert multiplication by a cosine in time into the half-weighted sum of two shifted Fourier spectra centered at the modulation frequencies.

sections.section_title: Writing a Cosine Product as Two Complex-Exponential Shifts

prompt_blocks.text: Given $y(t)=m(t)\cos(2\omega_1 t)$, which time-domain identity matches the Euler expansion?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the cosine factor. Use Euler's identity to split $\cos(2\omega_1 t)$ into two equal exponential terms, then multiply by $m(t)$.
Distributing $m(t)$ gives $\frac{1}{2}m(t)e^{j2\omega_1 t}+\frac{1}{2}m(t)e^{-j2\omega_1 t}$, which is choice B.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $z(t)=A p(t)\cos(\Omega t)$, which time-domain identity matches the Euler expansion?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cosine still expands into two equal exponential terms, and the amplitude $A$ stays attached to both halves.
So the correct rewrite is the half-weighted sum in choice D.

sections.section_title: Computing the Two Half-Weighted Shifted Spectra

prompt_blocks.text: Given $x(t)$ has CTFT $X(j\omega)$, what is $Y(j\omega)$ for $y(t)=x(t)\cos(3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the cosine-modulation rule: $\cos(3t)$ becomes two complex-exponential modulations, so the spectrum is two half-weighted copies of $X(j\omega)$ shifted to $\omega-3$ and $\omega+3$.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $e^{-t}u(t)$ has CTFT $\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$, what is the CTFT of $e^{-t}u(t)\cos(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Apply the same cosine-modulation formula with $\omega_0=2$. The original spectrum is copied to $\omega-2$ and $\omega+2$, and each copy keeps the factor $\frac{1}{2}$.

sections.section_title: Applying Cosine Modulation to a Standard Transform Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Given $e^{-2t}u(t)$ has CTFT $\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, what is the CTFT of $e^{-2t}u(t)\cos(5t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use cosine modulation: multiplying by $\cos(5t)$ gives two shifted copies of the spectrum, each with weight $1/2$.
Substitute $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$ into both shifted terms.

prompt_blocks.text: Given $e^{-4t}u(t)$ has CTFT $\frac{1}{4+j\omega}$, what is the CTFT of $e^{-4t}u(t)\cos(2t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Cosine modulation turns the product into two half-weighted shifts of the known spectrum.
Now substitute the base pair $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{4+j\omega}$ into both shifts.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Cosine Modulation as Two Shifted Spectral Copies

prompt_blocks.text: Which description best matches $Y(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2}\left[X(j(\omega-3))+X(j(\omega+3))\right]$?

choice_blocks.text: The spectrum has two copies centered at $\omega=0$ and $\omega=3$.
The spectrum has two copies centered at $\omega=\pm 3$, but there is no $\frac{1}{2}$ factor.
The spectrum contains only one shifted copy centered at $\omega=3$.
The spectrum is two half-height copies of $X(j\omega)$ centered at $\omega=\pm 3$.

questions.correct_answer: Two half-height copies of $X(j\omega)$ centered at $\omega=\pm 3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Cosine modulation produces two shifted spectra, one at $\omega-3$ and one at $\omega+3$, and each copy keeps the $\frac{1}{2}$ weight. The formula does not leave the spectrum unchanged, collapse the two shifts into $0$ and $3$, or remove the half factor.

prompt_blocks.text: Which description best matches $Y(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2}\left[X(j(\omega-5))+X(j(\omega+5))\right]$?

choice_blocks.text: The spectrum is two half-height copies of $X(j\omega)$ centered at $\omega=\pm 5$.
The spectrum has two copies centered at $\omega=0$ and $\omega=5$.
The spectrum contains only one shifted copy centered at $\omega=5$.
The spectrum has two copies centered at $\omega=\pm 5$, but the $\frac{1}{2}$ factor is missing.

questions.correct_answer: Two half-height copies of $X(j\omega)$ centered at $\omega=\pm 5$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: This is the same cosine-modulation pattern as the worked example, with the carrier frequency changed from $3$ to $5$. The result is still two half-weighted copies of the original spectrum, centered at $\omega=\pm 5$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert differentiation in time into multiplication by j omega in the continuous-time Fourier transform domain to compute spectra without redoing the transform integral.

sections.section_title: Transforming a First Derivative from a Known Spectrum

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}e^{j3t}$ if $e^{j3t}\leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega-3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the derivative property: multiply the known spectrum by $j\omega$. The $\delta$ spike is at $\omega=3$, so the multiplier becomes $j3$ at that spike.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}e^{-j4t}$ if $e^{-j4t}\leftrightarrow 2\pi\delta(\omega+4)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The derivative property again says to multiply the known spectrum by $j\omega$. Here the spike is at $\omega=-4$, so the multiplier becomes $-j4$ at that spike.

sections.section_title: Applying the j omega Factor to a Known Transform Pair

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}\cos(4t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the known pair $\cos(4t)\leftrightarrow \pi[\delta(\omega-4)+\delta(\omega+4)]$ and multiply by $j\omega$.
At $\omega=4$, the factor is $j4$, and at $\omega=-4$, the factor is $-j4$. That gives $4j\pi[\delta(\omega-4)-\delta(\omega+4)]$ after simplification.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(3\cos(2t)\bigr)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Keep the coefficient $3$ attached and use $\cos(2t)\leftrightarrow \pi[\delta(\omega-2)+\delta(\omega+2)]$.

The $\delta$ spikes evaluate the frequency factor at $\omega=\pm2$, so the positive spike gets $+j2$ and the negative spike gets $-j2$. Multiplying by $3$ gives $6j\pi[\delta(\omega-2)-\delta(\omega+2)]$.

sections.section_title: Combining Linearity with the Time-Derivative Property

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(4\cos(3t)+2\cos(7t)\bigr)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the derivative across the sum, then apply the derivative property to each cosine term separately. The coefficient-frequency products are $4\cdot 3=12$ and $2\cdot 7=14$.

prompt_blocks.text: What is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(-3\cos(2t)+5\cos(4t)\bigr)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the weighted sum first, then use the derivative property on each cosine term. The first coefficient stays negative, so the $2$-frequency pair keeps the negative sign.

sections.section_title: Using the Time-Derivative Property to Avoid the Transform Integral

prompt_blocks.text: Without evaluating any transform integrals, what is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}(3\cos(4t)-\sin(2t)+e^{j5t})$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a derivative of a sum built from known pairs, so split the sum and use the time-derivative property term by term instead of starting an integral.

The cosine term produces the signed $j\pi$ pair, the negative sine term produces the real two-spike pair, and the complex exponential produces a single shifted spike scaled by $j5$. Combining them gives the correct spectrum.

prompt_blocks.text: Without evaluating any transform integrals, what is the CTFT of $\frac{d}{dt}(2\cos(4t)+\sin(7t)-e^{j2t})$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is again a composite derivative with known pairs, so split the sum first and then apply the derivative property to each part separately.

The cosine term becomes the signed $j\pi$ pair, the positive sine term becomes a real two-spike pair, and the negative complex exponential becomes a negative $j$-scaled spike. Keep each coefficient attached to its own spectrum term.

entries.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
entries.lesson_core_move: Solve continuous-time Fourier transform problems by decomposing the signal into known transform pairs and selecting the appropriate property to assemble the resulting spectrum.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Identifying the Base Fourier Transform Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=5e^{-3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the decaying exponential multiplied by $u(t)$, which matches the stored pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$. The only extra feature is the outer factor 5, so first identify the base pair and then carry the coefficient through linearity.
Substitute $a=3$ and attach the coefficient 5. That gives $X(j\omega)=\frac{5}{3+j\omega}$.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=-2e^{-4t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The cue is still the one-sided decaying exponential, so it matches the same base pair $e^{-at}u(t)$. The negative coefficient stays attached to the spectrum by linearity; it does not change the decay constant.
Substitute $a=4$ and keep the factor $-2$ in front. The transform is $X(j\omega)=\frac{-2}{4+j\omega}$.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Decomposing a Signal into Known-Pair Terms

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)-3e^{-4t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the signal into the two known-pair terms $e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $-3e^{-4t}u(t)$ before doing any transform work. Then apply the pair $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$ to each term and carry the minus sign through by linearity.

Adding the two spectra gives $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}-\frac{3}{4+j\omega}$. The key step is the decomposition: once the sum is split into known-pair pieces, the transform is just the sum of the individual transforms.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=4e^{-t}u(t)-e^{-3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is already a sum of two known-pair terms, so split it first and keep the negative sign on the second term. Then use $e^{-at}u(t)\leftrightarrow \frac{1}{a+j\omega}$ on each piece and add the spectra.
So the final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=\frac{4}{1+j\omega}-\frac{1}{3+j\omega}$. The move is still decomposition before computation, not collapsing the time-domain terms into one expression.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Selecting the Property for Each Signal Modification

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=4e^{-3(t-2)}u(t-2)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Write the signal as $4x_0(t-2)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$. Linearity keeps the factor 4, and the delay of 2 contributes the phase factor $e^{-j2\omega}$.
So the transformed signal is the base spectrum multiplied by the scale factor and the delay factor.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=2e^{-5(t+1)}u(t+1)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t+1)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-5t}u(t)$. The factor 2 stays outside by linearity, and the advance by 1 gives the phase factor $e^{j\omega}$.
That means you use the shifted version of the known pair, not the unshifted one.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Combining Multiple Properties on a Modified Known Pair

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=2e^{-(t-2)}u(t-2)\cos(5t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t-2)\cos(5t)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $X_0(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$. Apply the delay first, then use cosine modulation to split the spectrum into the $\omega\pm5$ shifted copies.
Substitute the known pair into each shifted copy and keep the two terms separate so the delay phase stays attached to the correct frequency shift.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=2e^{-(t-1)}u(t-1)\cos(4t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Rewrite the signal as $2x_0(t-1)\cos(4t)$ with $x_0(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$. The delay contributes the phase factor, and cosine modulation splits the spectrum into the two shifted copies.
Substitute $X_0(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ into each copy and simplify. The correct answer keeps the delay factor attached to each shifted frequency term.

sections.lesson_title: Solving Transform Problems Using Known Pairs
sections.section_title: Assembling the Final Spectrum from Transformed Pieces

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=2e^{-(t-2)}u(t-2)\cos(4t)+e^{-2t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the signal into the delayed cosine-modulated piece and the plain exponential piece. Transform each part separately, then add the spectra at the end.
The final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=X_1(j\omega)+X_2(j\omega)$. The step is only assembly: keep each transformed piece intact and combine them at the end.

prompt_blocks.text: Find the Fourier transform of $x(t)=2e^{-(t-1)}u(t-1)\cos(5t)-3e^{-3t}u(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Split the signal into the delayed cosine-modulated term and the decaying exponential term. Transform each piece separately, keeping the minus sign on the second piece.
The final spectrum is $X(j\omega)=X_1(j\omega)+X_2(j\omega)$. Assemble the transformed pieces at the end and do not shift the unmodified exponential term.
